news.title: Democrats Within Striking Distance of Flipping Two Major Trump Strongholds
news.text: Two Senate races in states that President Donald Trump won decisively in 2024 are now rated as toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, as clashes in Iowa and Texas turn increasingly competitive, widening Democrats' potential path to a Senate majority. The rating changes come as Democrats seek to regain control of the Senate while edging into traditionally Republican territory, including Iowa and Texas, where Trump won by roughly 13 and 14 percentage points, respectively, in 2024. Democrats also saw movement in their favor in the gubernatorial contests, adding to signs of increasing competitiveness across the two states. In its update, Cook described the political landscape in Iowa as “uniquely challenging for the GOP.” While Republicans remain favored to hold many of the seats under their control, the shifting outlook in Iowa and Texas suggests the political map may be expanding beyond the traditional battleground states. Democrats need to maintain their seats and flip four to retake control of the Senate, as Republicans carry a 53-45 majority in the upper chamber. (Independent Senators Bernie Sanders and Angus King also caucus with the Democratic Party.) Cook's outlook also highlights the challenges Democrats face in defending their own battleground seats, including Michigan, where the open Senate race is also rated as a toss-up. “This news proves what people across this state already know: we are going to end 30 years of one-party rule and take back Texas,” Lone Star State Democrat James Talarico’s campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Newsweek about Cook's update. Newsweek also reached out to the campaigns of Texas Republican candidate Ken Paxton, along with Iowa's Josh Turek, a Democrat, and his Senate race foe Ashley Hinson, a Republican, for comment via email on Thursday. What To Know Democrats say concerns over the economy, Trump's standing with voters and a series of stronger-than-expected election results have improved their prospects, while Republicans maintain that the political environment will favor the GOP in November. High-profile primaries and recent polling have reshaped several midterm races, elevating new candidates and prompting several major election forecasters to revisit their ratings. The Cook Political Report has classified a handful of closely watched Senate races as “toss-ups,” including, Alaska, Maine, Ohio and Michigan, and on Thursday, shifted the Texas and Iowa Senate races to toss-up status. Both races were previously seen as “Lean Republican.” In the Iowa update, the forecaster said, “even though the GOP’s nominee Representative Ashley Hinson is one of their best recruits—and is running more competitively than retiring Senator Joni Ernst would have been—the political environment is uniquely challenging for the GOP here.” In Texas, Trump-endorsed Attorney General Paxton's primary defeat of Senator John Cornyn seems to have added uncertainty to a race once seen as reliably Republican. With Texas and Iowa shifted to toss-up status, Cook no longer lists any relatively tight Senate races as "Lean Republican." It rates three contests as "Lean Democrat," including North Carolina's open seat, currently held by Republicans. The Cook analysis also updated both of the states' gubernatorial races, updating Texas from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican," and Iowa from "toss-up" to "lean Democrat." All four of the statewide updates bode well for Democrats. With 75 days until the midterms, candidates are expected to pour millions into Iowa, Texas and other competitive contests as both parties fight for control of the Senate. Iowa Political Landscape Representative Hinson is battling state Representative Turek in the Iowa Senate race. They are running to succeed Republican Senator Joni Ernst, who chose not to run for reelection. Democrats haven't secured a Senate seat in the state since Tom Harkin's election in 2008. Iowa was viewed as a battleground for much of the 2000s, with former President Barack Obama carrying the state by about 10 points in 2008 and 6 points in 2012. But Trump performed well there in each of his presidential bids, winning by 10 points in 2016, 8 points in 2020 and 13 points in 2024. Republican Governor Kim Reynolds, who has led the state since 2017, is not seeking reelection. The last time a Democrat won Iowa’s governorship was in 2006, when Chet Culver was elected. Culver lost his reelection in 2010 to Republican Terry Branstad, and there's been a Republican in office ever since. Democrat Rob Sand is going up against Republican nominee Zach Lahn for the state office. In response to the updated rating, Turek said in an X post on Thursday morning, "We’ve always known this would be close, and now the experts agree: This is one of the closest Senate races in the country." He added, "Iowans are ready for change. We’re going to win this race in November and Push for Change!" Steffen Schmidt, emeritus professor of political science at Iowa State University, told Newsweek in an email, “It's true that the political environment in Iowa is very flexible and it is possible that the field has become competitive.” He added that both parties are taking the toss-up classification as “a challenge for them to mobilize voters.” However, Tim Hagle, associate professor in the Department of Political Science at the University of Iowa, told Newsweek in an email, “I'm sure Cook [Political Report] has its reasons for the change, but I don't buy it.” He continued, “I think there's a chance the governor's race could go for [Rob] Sand (Dem) and the Senate race for Hinson (Rep). Both races will be determined by Iowa's No Party voters (independents) and they are very capable of splitting their vote.” Iowa Senate Race Turek is a two-time Paralympic gold medalist and state House member, first elected in 2022. Obama endorsed him in a late-July video, while Trump has endorsed Hinson, who was first elected in 2020 after serving in the state House and working as a journalist. Fox News Power Rankings also rates the Iowa Senate race as a toss-up, while Sabato's Crystal Ball continues to classify the contest as “leans Republican.” Turnout in both parties' Senate primaries in the state surpassed 2022 levels, with 206,786 ballots cast in the Republican primary and 192,136 in the Democratic primary, compared with 198,858 Republican ballots and 158,745 Democratic ballots four years ago. Recent polling shows a tight race in Iowa, with RealClearPolling's average giving Hinson a lead of less than 1 percentage point over Turek, 47 percent to 46.3 percent. An August Emerson poll also found Hinson with a slight lead, 47.5 percent to 45 percent. She was viewed favorably by 44 percent of respondents and unfavorably by 40 percent, while Turek was viewed favorably by 42 percent and unfavorably by 27 percent. It surveyed 712 likely voters from August 2 to August 4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. An earlier Fox News poll of 1,003 Iowa registered voters found Turek leading Hinson 50 percent to 46 percent, with 4 percent undecided. The poll was conducted from June 23 to June 27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A June New York Times/Siena College poll found Hinson with a 2-point lead, 48 percent to Turek’s 46 percent. About 5 percent of likely voters were unsure. The poll, however, found Turek holding stronger favorability ratings than Hinson, with 46 percent viewing him favorably and 19 percent unfavorably, compared with 41 percent favorable and 34 percent unfavorable for Hinson. The poll of 600 likely voters was conducted from June 15 to June 17 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. Texas Political Landscape The GOP's decades-long hold on Texas statewide offices will be tested in November, with the Senate race between Paxton and Talarico nearly deadlocked in polls. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Republican Ted Cruz. Trump carried Texas in each of his three presidential runs, winning the state by roughly 9 percentage points in 2016, 6 points in 2020 and nearly 14 points in 2024. Still, Texas has become increasingly competitive in recent election cycles as population growth and higher turnout in major metropolitan areas have narrowed some statewide margins. Paxton used the rating change to urge supporters to donate and get involved as he campaigns against Talarico, directing voters to go to his campaign website. The Texas governor's race is one of 36 gubernatorial contests in 2026, a cycle that includes several other high-profile open-seat races in states like Michigan, Alaska, Iowa, Wisconsin, Nevada and Georgia. Governor Greg Abbott is a strong conservative and staunch ally of Trump who was first elected to the state's top office in 2014 and reelected in 2018 and 2022. A fourth term would put Abbott on track to become the longest-serving governor in Texas history, surpassing Rick Perry, who served from 2000 to 2015. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a lawyer who was sworn in to the Texas House in 2017, secured the Democratic nomination in March. Texas Senate Race Texas has become a key battleground in the fight for Senate control, with the closely contested race between Paxton and Talarico offering Democrats a rare opportunity to compete in a state that has not elected a Democrat statewide in more than three decades. “Ken Paxton is bought by billionaire mega-donors and special interests, runs away every time a reporter asks him a question, and has spent his career enriching himself at the expense of working Texans. Texans are tired of this broken, corrupt political system and are ready to elect a leader who will fight for working people,” Ennis said in a statement to Newsweek. Fox News Power Rankings earlier this week moved Texas into the "toss up” column, though Sabato's Crystal Ball continues to rate the race as "Lean Republican." RealClearPolling aggregate average puts Talarico up by 1.2 percentage points, 46 percent to Paxton’s 44.8 percent. Polls go back and forth on who leads in the Lone Star State, often with statistical leads within the margin of error. Surveys show both Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign and among different pollsters. A recent Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters puts the Senate race in a near dead heat, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 percent supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted from August 9 to August 11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. An earlier Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent backed Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted from July 23 to July 27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: The Cook Political Report shifted Iowa and Texas Senate races to "toss-up" status on Thursday.
news.author: Mandy Taheri

news.title: 'We are going to collapse this regime': Inside the US plan to target Iran's economy
news.text: President Donald Trump vowed “economic D-day” against Iran and consequences for countries providing a “lifeline” to the country, as the U.S. intensifies economic pressure in its campaign.“No one has given the Islamic Republic of Iran a greater opportunity to make a Deal than me. TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it. Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.MORE ON THE PLAN | Iran dismisses Trump’s ‘Economic D-Day’ threat amid pressure for deal to end warWhile the specific details weren’t known immediately, a U.S. official said new action is expected.“We are going to collapse this regime,” Treasury Sec. Scott Bessent said in an interview with CNBC, warning other countries that insist on doing business with Iran will face the force of the U.S. government.“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat. These maniacs are on the ropes, and these HISTORIC MEASURES will cripple them and their ability to project terror worldwide,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.The announcement comes as the President’s focus appears to be on economic levers at this point in the conflict, rather than diplomatic or military means.The administration’s focus is on squeezing Iran economically versus militarily, according to a U.S. official, though the president maintains military options.The administration believes Iran is facing internal strife, particularly with its economy, and that the military campaign has helped put a chokehold on it, according to a senior administration official, who suggested ahead of the announcement Iran will be forced to make a deal.“If we are doing the maximum economic pressure then that means likely there will not be a large scale kinetic restart but I would emphasize that is for now,” Bessent told CNBC.IRAN WAR | As Hormuz blockade continues, Trump appears ready to wait for Iran to show interest in a dealEarlier in the week, as U.S. military strikes have appeared to pause, Trump said there were no conversations going on with Iran. While there were “positive discussions” according to a source familiar, “President Trump has decided to wait and asked his team to not engage until Iran is ready to make a deal.”However, Iran is dismissing President Donald Trump’s threat of an “Economic D-Day.”“The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said on X. “Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. U.S. economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide.”But Vice President JD Vance called it a “new phase” where economic pressure is “the most effective tool,” in an interview with The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show.“And this is a delicate dance because we apply economic pressure to them they’re gonna try to apply economic pressure to us but what has been true over the past couple of weeks they’ve felt a lot more pressure than we have. We’re gonna keep that going because we think that’s the best way to ultimately accomplish the final objective here, we have to go back to the very beginning the president said Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” he said to the hosts.Vance said they’re trying to “…create a change reality on the ground where not just we can say with confidence their facilities have been destroyed, we can also say with confidence they’re never going to try to rebuild and that’s the phase that we’re in now.”The impact for other nations remains to be seen. Major historical trading partners for Iran include China, the UAE, Turkey and Iraq.“Sanctions and pressure will not help resolve the issue,” Chinese ministry of foreign affairs spokesperson Lin Jian said in a press briefing.China, whose leader Trump expects to visit the U.S. next month, has retaliated against past U.S. trade crackdowns.“That type of retaliation and response is very likely. The Iranians know that they are willing to sustain an enormous amount of pain, economic pain. They've shown that for decades,” said Amb. Daniel Shapiro, a distinguished fellow with the Atlantic Council, former ambassador to Israel in the Obama administration and former deputy assistant secretary of defense for the Middle East in the Biden administration.The UAE got ahead of the President’s announcement, declaring Wednesday that it would cut financial ties with Iran after alleging it fired more ballistic missiles towards the Gulf nation.“I don't take that announcement as at face value as a an indication that Gulf states are fully embracing this. They might be trying to avoid getting on the wrong side of Trump in this moment. They certainly feel a great sense of grievance toward Iran because Iran has attacked them when most of them were not combatants in this war and corrupted their economies, but they are likely at some point to sense a declining U.S. commitment, and they will then seek to cut their own deals with Iran and keep those channels open so that they're able to do so when the when the moment arrives,” Shapiro said.
news.summary: The U.S. is planning a campaign of "maximum economic pressure" on Iran and its allies, U.S. officials say.

news.title: Michael Cohen, Trump’s former fixer-turned-enemy, is hosting the president on his radio show
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is expected to appear Thursday on the radio show of his former fixer-turned-foe Michael Cohen, making a public reunion with the man who once called him a “Cheeto-dusted cartoon villain” and testified against him both in court and before Congress.

Cohen, who served prison time for his role in what he said was covering up Trump’s “dirty deeds,” confirmed that the Republican president will appear in a taped interview airing on his 77 WABC program Thursday evening and Sunday.

In an interview with CNN shortly before the interview’s scheduled air time, Cohen said it would be a “doozy,” but he declined to address his past criticism of Trump.

“I refuse to be pulled back into yesterday’s news and yesterday’s headline,” he said.

To the many people asking, “How is this possible?” he said, “The answer is that we forgave.”

The truce with Cohen makes him the latest in a long line of Trump loyalists who have had public falling-outs with the president but found themselves back in his good graces. Other recent examples include Elon Musk and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

But the split from Cohen was perhaps the most personal. Cohen once boasted that he would “take a bullet” for Trump and was by Trump’s side during his political rise. After their public breakup, Cohen’s testimony in Trump’s 2024 criminal hush-money trial instead paved the way for Trump’s criminal conviction just as he was trying to make his political comeback.

Cohen has since criticized prosecutors in the case and has said he and Trump have started to reconcile.

The White House did not comment on Cohen’s statements or confirm the appearance, but Trump’s official schedule showed him taping a radio interview Thursday morning.

In a long post on his online newsletter Thursday promoting the interview, Cohen said that although his relationship with Trump became “political blood sport,” there were 15 years of close friendship between them.

“The good times don’t cease to have existed because the bad times came afterward,” Cohen wrote.

Simply, he said: “We forgave.”

Trump has made no warm public statements about Cohen but in a series of social media posts this year linked to some of his former lawyer’s comments saying he felt pressured by prosecutors to testify against Trump in the criminal hush money case and a civil fraud case.

In 2024, Cohen was the star witness in Trump’s criminal hush money trial, which resulted in a 34-count felony conviction.

Over days of probing questioning by prosecutors, followed by bruising cross-examination, Cohen placed the then-Republican candidate at the center of schemes during the 2016 presidential election to stifle accounts from an adult film actor and former Playboy model who said they had sexual encounters with Trump.

Cohen testified that Trump promised to reimburse the lawyer for the money he fronted and was constantly updated about behind-the-scenes efforts to bury stories feared to be harmful to the campaign.

“What I was doing, I was doing at the direction of and benefit of Mr. Trump,” Cohen testified.

Cohen’s testimony at the time appeared to be the final breach in a once-close relationship between the lawyer and his client that was tested in dramatic fashion in 2018 when FBI agents searched Cohen’s office, home and hotel room.

Cohen later pleaded guilty to lying to Congress about a Trump Tower project in Russia as well as to campaign finance violations in which he implicated Trump in payments that went to Stormy Daniels, an adult film star, and Playboy Playmate Karen MacDougal. He was sentenced to three years in prison.

Since his trial testimony, though, Cohen has sung a different tune as he’s moved closer to Trump, insisting that he had testified under duress.

“I felt pressured and coerced to only provide information and testimony that would satisfy the government’s desire to build the cases against and secure a judgment and convictions against President Trump,” he wrote in a Substack post in January.

Cohen testified before Congress in 2019, alleging Trump had a history of misrepresenting the value of assets to gain favorable loan terms and tax benefits.

He gave similar testimony in a 2023 civil fraud trial in New York that found Trump and his companies engaged in fraud by exaggerating his wealth for decades. A New York appeals court later threw out a $550 million judgment against Trump in that case. Trump has asked a court to overturn the remaining parts of the case.

In his tell-all memoir in 2020, “Disloyal: The True Story of the Former Personal Attorney to President Donald J. Trump,” Cohen was unsparing, calling Trump an “organized crime don” and “master manipulator.”

But, foreshadowing their later rapprochement, Cohen also wrote that he still cared for Trump, writing, “I had and still have a lot of affection for him.”

news.title: Melania Trump addresses mysterious White House absence with 5-word comeback
news.text:
Melania Trump broke cover in the White House Rose Garden on Thursday, more than 30 days after she made her last public appearance at the FIFA World Cup Final in New Jersey on July 19.

The 56-year-old arrived to share an update on her Fostering the Future campaign, dressed in a bright red Dior pencil skirt paired with a blue Michael Kors collared shirt and red suede Manolo heels.

Return to public life

The First Lady began with a five-word remark, referring to the increased media attention surrounding her lengthy absence. "I heard you missed me," she quipped as she stood at the lectern, before adding: "Here I am."

Melania then launched into a speech about her Fostering the Future initiative, which will expand its network following a $2 million donation from IndyCar and Fox Corporation to fund scholarships at Indiana University and Purdue University.

The initiative encompassed 26 universities in the US, including the University of Texas, the University of North Carolina, and Pepperdine University. 

"The greatest investment America can make is not in technology, infrastructure, or capital markets. It's our children," Melania said.

Learn more about Melania below...

"But America's greatest competitive advantage remains in its own people. Tomorrow's leaders are sitting in classrooms today, including those growing up in foster care. Their capability is no less remarkable."

She added: "Education is the one asset that can never be taken away. It is the foundation upon which confidence is built, opportunity is created, and the future is invented."

Melania concluded by wishing luck to the drivers of the upcoming Freedom 250 Grand Prix, which will take place in Washington, D.C. over the weekend.

After her speech, Melania was handed a custom metallic racing helmet inscribed with "Melania Be Best Fostering the Future" by IndyCar drivers Scott Dixon, Alexander Rossi, Graham Rayhall and Scott McLaughlin. She did not put it on, and instead handed it over to an aide. 

Melania's disappearance

Melania's lengthy absence has drawn scrutiny in recent days, with several outlets reporting that she has only made 38 public appearances in 2026. The mother of one skipped the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham on July 28, and the White House Correspondents' Dinner on July 24.

A senior advisor clarified to NBC News that her recent absence from public life was because she "prioritizes results over appearances", and her team announced that Melania had been working behind the scenes on an initiative to reunite children with their families amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Donald Trump's 35-year-old aide, Natalie Harp, has raised eyebrows in recent weeks after Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff highlighted her unwavering loyalty at a rally on August 16. 

"He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie," Jon quipped, prompting a dramatic response from the White House via Donald's director of communications, Steven Cheung.

"Jon [Ossoff] has to be the biggest [expletive] loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard-working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he's a miserable person who hates this country," Steven wrote on X.

According to the book Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, written by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, Donald said during his second term that Natalie was the "only one who loved him as much as his wife and his kids".

news.title: How Major US Stock Indexes Fared Aug. 20
news.text:
The relief that swept the bond market just a day earlier disappeared as oil prices, worries about high inflation and the U.S. government’s debt kept rising.

That helped knock the U.S. stock market to its worst loss in three weeks on Thursday, and Walmart led the way on concerns about its upcoming profits.

Treasury yields climbed after the price of Brent crude rose 2.4 percent following President Donald Trump’s latest threat to Iran.

On Thursday:

The S&P 500 fell 66.82 points, or 0.9 percent, to 7,641.16.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 703.84 points, or 1.3 percent, to 52,759.21.

The Nasdaq composite fell 263.92 points, or 1 percent, to 26,067.17.

The Russell 2000 index of smaller companies fell 40.51 points, or 1.3 percent, to 2,992.43.

For the week:

The S&P 500 is down 144.60 points, or 1.9 percent.

The Dow is down 973.20 points, or 1.8 percent.

The Nasdaq is down 662 points, or 2.5 percent.

The Russell 2000 is down 75.98 points, or 2.5 percent.

For the year:

The S&P 500 is up 795.66 points, or 11.6 percent.

The Dow is up 4,695.92 points, or 9.8 percent.

The Nasdaq is up 2,825.18 points, or 12.2 percent.

The Russell 2000 is up 510.53 points, or 20.6 percent.
